questions.question: Which statement gives the working description of $\mathbb R$ used in Math I: Calculus?
options: The complete ordered number system represented by the real line
The finite ordered list of all positive rational numbers
The number system obtained by allowing a zero denominator
The unordered collection of all subsets of rational numbers

questions.question: Which notation denotes the set of all real numbers?
options: $\mathbb{Q}$
$\mathbb{R}$
$\mathbb{Z}$
$\mathbb{N}$

questions.question: Which of the following numbers is real but not rational?
options: $\sqrt{2}$
The set $\mathbb{Q}$

questions.question: Which statement correctly classifies the integer $-3$ using the number-system inclusions?
options: It belongs to $\mathbb Z$ but not to $\mathbb Q$.
It belongs to $\mathbb Z$, $\mathbb Q$, and $\mathbb R$.
It belongs to $\mathbb Q$ but not to $\mathbb Z$.
It belongs to $\mathbb R$ but not to $\mathbb Q$.

questions.question: Which property of $\mathbb R$ expresses the completeness used in this course?
options: Every sequence of real numbers converges to a real limit
Every nonempty real set bounded above has a least upper bound
Every real number can be expressed as a ratio of integers
Every pair of integers has an integer quotient

questions.question: What role do real numbers play relative to rational numbers?
options: They remove all irrational numbers from arithmetic.
They make limits impossible to define.
They replace sequences by unordered sets.
They complete the rational numbers by filling limiting gaps.

questions.question: Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R$ be nonempty and bounded above. What does completeness guarantee?
options: The set $E$ has a largest element in $E$.
The set $E$ has a smallest element in $E$.
Every upper bound of $E$ is a rational in $E$.
The set $E$ has a unique least upper bound in $\mathbb R$.

questions.question: How are the real numbers split by rationality?
options: A real number can be neither rational nor irrational.
Every irrational number is excluded from $\mathbb{R}$.
Every real number is either rational or irrational.
Only rational numbers can be limits of rational sequences.

questions.question: Which statement describes the density of $\mathbb Q$ in $\mathbb R$?
options: Every bounded real set has a least upper bound.
Between any two distinct real numbers lies a rational number.
Every real number can be written as a ratio of integers.
Every sequence of rational numbers is eventually constant.

questions.question: Which statement best captures the phrase “filling in all limiting gaps”?
options: Rational numbers stop being numbers inside $\mathbb{R}$.
Every sequence of rational numbers is automatically finite.
Limits of rational sequences become exact numerical objects.
Irrational numbers are removed from the number system.

questions.question: For $x=10$ and $\varepsilon=0.03$, which positive integer $M$ verifies the Archimedean inequality $M\varepsilon>x$?
What can safely be concluded about $\sqrt2$?
options: It is rational because decimal approximations exist.
It is a real number and it is irrational.
It is undefined because no rational squares to $2$.
It is an integer strictly between $1$ and $2$.

questions.question: What is the relationship between $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R}$?
options: $\mathbb{Q}\subseteq\mathbb{R}$
$\mathbb{R}\subseteq\mathbb{Q}$
they are disjoint
$\mathbb{Q}=\mathbb{R}$

questions.question: Between any two distinct real numbers, how many rational numbers lie?
options: Infinitely many
Exactly one
None
Exactly two

questions.question: If $x<y$ and $z>0$ are real numbers, which relation must hold?
options: $xz>yz$
$xz=yz$
$xz<yz$
$x+z>y+z$

questions.question: Which conclusion connects completeness of $\mathbb R$ to the monotone convergence theorem?
options: Every bounded increasing real sequence converges to its supremum.
Every sequence of real numbers converges to a finite value.
Every bounded real sequence must be increasing.
Every rational sequence has a rational limit.

questions.question: Which classification is possible for $\sqrt2$?
options: Rational but not real
Neither real nor irrational
Natural and equal to $2$
Real and irrational

questions.question: Which set contains $\pi$?
options: $\mathbb Q\setminus\mathbb Z$
$\mathbb Z$
$\mathbb N$
$\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q$

questions.question: What does it mean that real numbers complete the rational numbers?
options: They remove all rational numbers
They make every sequence divergent.
They consist only of integers
They fill limiting gaps left by rationals.

questions.question: Which statement follows for every $x\in\mathbb R$?
options: $x$ is both rational and irrational
$x$ is always a natural number
$x$ is either an integer or not real
$x$ is rational or irrational
